```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This guide takes you from a four-product horizontal merger in the app to a
saved R script that reproduces it. You need basic R and the current
`competitiontoolbox` package; this example uses `antitrust` 0.99.43 or later.
No Bayesian estimation is involved.

## Open the app and choose the question

If needed, follow the [installation instructions](https://github.com/luciu5/competitiontoolbox#installation)
in a fresh R session. Launch the app locally:

```{r launch, eval=FALSE}
library(competitiontoolbox)
ct_shiny()
```

This opens a browser interface. Stop the app with the R console's Stop button
or Escape when finished. Ordinary use does not require Pandoc, TeX or CmdStan.
The optional hosted app may run a different version from your installed copy.

From **Introduction**, choose **Mergers > Horizontal**. Set these controls
explicitly, since a browser may retain earlier choices:

| Control | Choice |
|:--|:--|
| Calibration | market elasticity and 1 or more margins |
| Market elasticity | -1 |
| Competitive interaction | Bertrand |
| Demand | logit |

The question is: what happens when Firm1 acquires Firm2, leaving Firm3's
existing two-product portfolio intact?

## Understand the input rows

Enter or verify the following rows under **Enter Inputs**. Prices and quantities
use consistent arbitrary units. Margins are proportions of price: .25 means
25%, not 25 currency units.

```{r inputs}
simdata <- data.frame(
  product = paste0("Prod", 1:4),
  price = rep(10, 4), quantity = c(40, 30, 20, 10),
  margin = rep(.25, 4),
  owner_pre = c("Firm1", "Firm2", "Firm3", "Firm3"),
  owner_post = c("Firm1", "Firm1", "Firm3", "Firm3"),
  cost_change = rep(0, 4)
)
knitr::kable(simdata)
```

The default post-merger owners already describe the acquisition. Firm3 owns both
Prod3 and Prod4 before and after it. Treating those products as separate firms
would answer a different economic question. Quantities become conditional
inside-market shares in this Logit example; changing to a revenue-based model
requires checking its input definitions again.

Click **Simulate**. Inspect **Messages**, then **Diagnostics**, before reading
**Summary** or **Details**. Calibration fits a common demand system, so the
fitted margins need not reproduce every supplied margin exactly. Compare the
input-versus-fit discrepancies before using the result in advice or a report.
Finite output alone does not certify a good empirical fit.

## Reproduce the same market with public R functions

The following is a compact equivalent of this app scenario. The app's **R Code**
tab includes its own serialized input table and extraction commands; copy that
whole script for your actual analysis rather than trying to reuse browser state.

```{r simulate}
library(antitrust)
upstream_spec <- antitrust::model_spec(
  demand = "logit", conduct = "bertrand", variant = "alm"
)
fit <- antitrust::calibrate(
  demand = upstream_spec,
  prices = simdata$price,
  shares = simdata$quantity / sum(simdata$quantity),
  margins = simdata$margin,
  ownerPre = 1 * outer(simdata$owner_pre, simdata$owner_pre, "=="),
  mktElast = -1,
  insideSize = sum(simdata$quantity), labels = simdata$product
)
simres <- antitrust::simulate(
  fit,
  ownerPost = 1 * outer(simdata$owner_post, simdata$owner_post, "=="),
  mcDelta = simdata$cost_change
)
```

```{r results}
result <- data.frame(
  product = simdata$product,
  price_pre = as.numeric(antitrust::calcPrices(simres, preMerger = TRUE)),
  price_post = as.numeric(antitrust::calcPrices(simres, preMerger = FALSE)),
  share_post = as.numeric(antitrust::calcShares(simres, preMerger = FALSE))
)
result$price_change_pct <- 100 * (result$price_post / result$price_pre - 1)
result$inside_share_post_pct <- 100 * result$share_post / sum(result$share_post)
knitr::kable(result, digits = 3)
```

`price_change_pct` compares each product with its own pre-merger price. Shares
are fractions of the modeled market including the outside option, so they need
not sum to one across the four displayed products. The supplied input quantities
were normalized within the inside market; the fitted outside share changes that
denominator. `inside_share_post_pct` rescales the four displayed products to
100% and matches the app's **Details** quantity-share convention. For example,
raw share .28627 becomes about 37.589% within the inside market.
The app's industry price-change summary sums product percentage
changes times the **raw full-market post-merger shares** (`share_post`),
without rescaling them to sum to one.
It is not the percentage change of an unweighted average price, nor a draw-wise
uncertainty interval.

```{r weighted-change}
c(app_industry_price_change_pct = sum(
  result$price_change_pct * result$share_post
), outside_share_post = 1 - sum(result$share_post))
```

In **Summary**, positive **Consumer Harm** means consumers lose; a negative
number means benefit. Positive **Producer Benefit** means producers gain.
Parentheses report these measures as percentages of post-merger revenues.
**Elasticities** describes modeled responses, while **Diagnostics** describes
calibration and solution information. Neither establishes that the assumed
conduct or demand family is correct for your case.

As one controlled sensitivity, set Prod1's **Cost Changes** to `-.04` and rerun.
This is a 4% reduction in marginal cost, not four price units. Keep the other
rows unchanged. Compare the resulting prices with the original merger and
record which input changed. Each run starts from the entered pre-merger market;
this edit does not accumulate a second cost change on the previous run.

## Save and replay your analysis

Open **R Code**, copy **all** the text, paste it into a plain text file named
`merger-example.R`, and save it locally. The app provides copied code, not a
file download button. The script defines `simdata`, constructs the selected
model, calibrates `fit`, and computes `simres` without Shiny reactive objects.
Append this provenance line to the saved script:

```{r provenance, eval=FALSE}
sessionInfo()
```

Run the saved file in a fresh R session, including from a directory outside the
package checkout:

```{bash replay, eval=FALSE}
Rscript --vanilla /path/to/merger-example.R
```

Compare prices under identical inputs and controls. The copied script's
`summary()` defaults to full-market shares, whereas the app's **Details** table
shows inside-only shares. This is a denominator difference, not a different
equilibrium. After running the copied script, obtain directly comparable columns:

```{r app-details-comparison}
raw_share_post <- antitrust::calcShares(simres, preMerger = FALSE)
data.frame(price_post = antitrust::calcPrices(simres, preMerger = FALSE),
           app_inside_share_post_pct = 100 * raw_share_post / sum(raw_share_post))
```

Compare unrounded R values when diagnosing discrepancies, since the screen
rounds its tables. Save a separate script or clearly named input table
for the cost-reduction alternative. Copy its updated R Code as well.

If the script fails, first check the **Messages** tab, your installed package
versions, and that you copied the complete script. If a warning concerns fit,
inspect the supplied margins and elasticity; changing the model is a substantive
assumption, not a formatting fix.

## Continue with the relevant economic guide

The app's **Numerical Simulations** tabs browse stored research summaries and
figures. They do not launch a fresh Monte Carlo study for your current inputs.
See [Taragin and Loudermilk (2019)](https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.30872.85760/1)
and [Sheu and Taragin (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1111/1756-2171.12385)
for those studies.

For a script-based horizontal workflow, read
[antitrust's Workflow](https://github.com/luciu5/antitrust/blob/master/vignettes/Workflow.Rmd).
For other tasks, use the linked supply-chain guides in
[vertical](https://github.com/luciu5/vertical#readme) or the
[trade tariff guide](https://github.com/luciu5/trade/blob/master/vignettes/Reference.Rmd).
These links lead to maintained source guides; they do not require building a
website to use the package.
